channel.title: Daily Recap — 🔬 AI Research
channel.description: What happened in 🔬 AI Research, recapped daily from subscribed feeds.

item.title: PHP's botched disclosure postmortem: how a leak turned a security release into chaos
item.description:
If you run anything on PHP, yesterday and today were the days to drop everything and patch. The PHP 8.x security releases fix two remote code execution vulnerabilities — the PHP2Shell flaws discovered by AI agents — and the situation turned ugly because the coordinated disclosure process leaked. CVE IDs started circulating on forums and social media a day early, on October 20th, with a wrong release time and a bogus CVSS score of 10.0 (the real score is 9.2). Attackers had exploits circulating since the night before the patch dropped.

The PHP Foundation has now published a frank account of what went wrong and what changes next. Simon Willison walks through the postmortem: the leak effectively gave attackers a head start while leaving defenders scrambling, and AWS analysts confirmed exploit attempts in the wild as early as October 17. For anyone managing web infrastructure, the takeaways are to patch immediately across the entire PHP 8.x line and to watch for how the Foundation reforms its disclosure process so this doesn't happen again.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security

item.title: Claude Mods flips the agent harness: the attention interface faces the human
item.description:
Latent.Space digs into Claude Mods, Anthropic's early experiment with what some are calling the Attention Interface — a provocative inversion of how AI agents are built. Today's agent harnesses face the machine: scaffolding, tools, and orchestration wrapped around the model to make it act on computers. Claude Mods turns that inside out, putting the harness on the human side instead, so the agent reaches out before you ask and works around your attention rather than demanding it.

The idea matters because proactive agents — Anthropic's Claude Duet launched the same day — raise a real design question: who manages whom? If agents are going to interrupt, propose, and act autonomously, the interface has to be built around human attention as the scarce resource. Claude Mods is an early sketch of that future, and for anyone building or deploying agents, it's the paradigm shift to watch: from copilots you summon to ambient helpers you supervise.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: Claude Mods: Flipping the Harness Inside Out

item.title: IBM's Granite Speech 5.0 promises faster, more accurate transcribe-translate-attribute
item.description:
IBM released Granite Speech 5.0, the latest in its open Granite family of speech models, with claims of better accuracy and speed across three tasks: transcription, translation, and attribution (identifying who said what and when). The release landed on Hugging Face with the usual open weights and technical write-up, continuing IBM's steady push to make enterprise-grade speech models available outside closed APIs.

For practitioners, the interesting part is the attribution angle — speaker diarization and source attribution remain genuinely hard problems in real-world audio, and a faster, more accurate open model there could matter for meeting intelligence, call centers, and accessibility tooling. As with any vendor benchmark, the claims deserve independent testing, but Granite's track record of solid, un-hyped releases makes this one worth a look for teams building speech pipelines.

Sources

  • Hugging Face Blog: Granite Speech 5.0: Transcribe, Translate, and Attribute more Accurately and Faster

item.title: Private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CAs compromised in major trust-store incident
item.description:
The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority certificates have been compromised — and the blast radius is enormous. These intermediates chain up to roots trusted by Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple, and Chrome's root programs, plus countless downstream trust stores. Any software that bundles a list of trusted certificates needs to be updated, and a GitHub repository is tracking which software has shipped fixes. Linux distributions need to update their ca-certificates packages, and in the Python world, patched releases are already out: uv 0.13.4, pip 26.2.2, and certifi 2026.10.19 all carry upgraded certificate lists.

A compromised intermediate CA is one of the worst outcomes in the web's trust model: anyone holding the private keys could mint certificates for arbitrary domains that browsers and OSes would accept as legitimate. If you run infrastructure, the move is to make sure your trust stores are current today — and this is exactly the kind of incident where automated, prompt patching matters more than any clever countermeasure.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise

item.title: Anthropic's leaked draft bill gets a lukewarm response as Zvi says it doesn't get why the bill was "unacceptable and troubling"
item.description:
Anthony Cimino offered what amounts to the closest thing to an official Anthropic response to the leaked draft AI bill that Zvi covered over the weekend — and Zvi's verdict is blunt: Anthropic does not understand why the draft was unacceptable and troubling. The post digs into the disconnect between how the company views its legislative effort and how it actually reads to everyone else.

This matters because the AI-policy fight is moving from blog posts and open letters into actual legislation, and a leak like this sets the terms of debate before a bill is even formally introduced. When the most-read rationalist commentator on AI safety says a lab doesn't grasp the problem with its own draft, it's a signal that the bill's provisions — whatever the exact text — will face heavy scrutiny from the communities whose buy-in Anthropic would presumably want.

Sources

  • The Zvi: Anthropic Does Not Understand Why Its Draft Bill Was Unacceptable and Troubling

item.title: Mollick's new book and 30 months of AI progress in charts
item.description:
Ethan Mollick's new book is out, and he marked the occasion with a look back at what has changed in the 30 months since his last one — in charts. The post is essentially a visual tour of the AI exponential: the things that went from impossible to routine to boringly normal in two and a half years.

Mollick remains one of the clearest translators between AI capability jumps and what they mean for actual work. If you've felt whiplash trying to keep up, this is the retrospective format that makes the curve legible: not hype about the future, but receipts about the recent past. Worth reading alongside the book for anyone who advises organizations on how fast to adapt.

Sources

  • One Useful Thing: 30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts)

item.title: SF Compute's Evan Conrad on the programmable data center
item.description:
Latent.Space sat down with SF Compute's Evan Conrad to talk about the programmable data center: from GPU trading to physical settlement, independent markets, and programmable compute. The conversation covers how the company is turning raw compute into something that trades like a commodity — with markets, settlement, and programmatic access layered on top.

The compute market is quietly becoming one of the most important stories in AI infrastructure: who gets GPUs, at what price, and through what mechanism determines which labs and startups can actually train. SF Compute's thesis is that compute should behave less like rented servers and more like a financial market. Whether or not you buy the full vision, the framing is a useful lens on the economics behind the model race.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: The Programmable Data Center — Evan Conrad, SF Compute

item.title: Simon Willison vibe-codes a genuinely fun multiplayer RTS
item.description:
Simon Willison's latest vibe-coding experiment is Battle Drones, a Command & Conquer–style real-time strategy game — and unlike his previous experiments, he says this one is actually fun to play. He got there, he admits, by telling Claude to "make it a LOT more fun." The game iterates through versions from initial prototype to full sprites, varied terrain, and a dedicated fun update, and it supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state.

It's a nice datapoint on where AI-assisted coding is landing: a solo developer producing a playable, multiplayer game through iterated prompting. The audio-based sync for local multiplayer is the kind of scrappy solution that makes the writeup more interesting than the game itself. Playable in the browser if you want to try it.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: Battle Drones - a vibe coded RTS with audio-based multiplayer

item.title: Quiet news day, but new model drops: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, Mercury 3
item.description:
Latent.Space's AINews roundup called it honestly: not much happened today. The news was three new releases — DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, and Mercury 3 — with the caveat that none of them are going to be in super wide use just yet.

It's still a useful snapshot of the current release cadence: fast, incremental model drops that land with details but without broad deployment. For anyone tracking the frontier, these are names to file away; expect the wider rollout and real benchmarking to tell the story over the coming days.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: [AINews] not much happened today

item.title: Zvi sorts signal from hype on Goodfire's interpretability claim
item.description:
Zvi Mowshowitz published a lengthy response to Nick Cammarata's Goodfire post claiming neural networks are "already clean" — that apparent polysemanticity is mostly recursive generalization, not superposition, and that roughly 90% of neurons in models like Qwen3-32B have one main job. It's the most careful adjudication yet of the claim that has electrified the field.

His verdict lands in the middle: the work is solid and meaningful, telling us genuinely new and important things about how LLMs and minds form and operate, and it reduces our estimates of some task difficulties. But the hype is out of hand — we did not get an apples-to-apples jump from ~1.7% to 90% interpretability, and the claim that mechanistic interpretability is now nearly solved, or that alignment will soon follow, is overstated.

What it does do, Zvi argues, is tell us how to go about useful interpretability tasks and change the outlook going forward. Great work, assuming it checks out — but everyone needs to take a chill pill before declaring the second coming of deep learning's Attention paper.

Sources

  • The Zvi: I Can See Everything

item.title: Import AI 477: the singularity has begun, says Anthropic's Aschenbrenner to the IMF
item.description:
Jack Clark's Import AI newsletter this week is largely his speech from the IMF's Per Jacobsson lecture in Bangkok on October 17th, where he told an audience of economists, bankers, and policymakers that we are in the early stages of the singularity — and they should expect significant, rapid change.

His evidence: AI systems are now doing science at the frontier, sometimes autonomously. On Humanity's Last Exam, top scores went from 8% at launch in January 2025 to 67.7% for Claude Opus 5.5 this week; on FrontierMath, from 2% to 94%. And in the new TheoPhysEval paper on unpublished theoretical physics problems, models not only scored high but found errors in the experts' own answers — "the teacher becomes the student." Inside Anthropic, researchers now produce almost 10x the code they did in the company's first four years.

The pitch to policymakers: AI-driven scientific invention will accelerate the whole pace of progress, bringing great wealth and potentially great peril, and nations need foresight and restraint now to share in the benefits. It's the clearest public statement yet of the "singularity is already here" thesis from inside a frontier lab.

Sources

  • Import AI: Import AI 477: In which I tell the IMF the Singularity has begun

item.title: New paper maps 33 emerging trends in AI agent evaluation
item.description:
A new paper from a Princeton group (Felix Chen, Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor, Arvind Narayanan) with collaborators from Stanford, the UK AI Safety Institute, and Brookings synthesizes 33 emerging trends in AI agent evaluation across three dimensions: the science and methods, the research agenda, and the evaluation ecosystem. It's aimed at helping new entrants upskill and giving evaluators, funders, and the public better questions to ask.

The core argument: agent evaluation is fundamentally harder than model evaluation. Evaluators must scrutinize entire trajectories, not just final outcomes — checking for shortcuts, tool misuse, and attribution of behavior to agent components. Benchmarks are getting expensive (some ExploitBench agents cost tens of thousands of dollars in credits), independent evaluators are losing access to model internals like chain-of-thought traces, and results in the lab don't reliably translate to real-world deployment — a METR trial even found agent coding tools increased task completion time.

The paper calls for open-world evaluations, observational data on real usage, and treating evaluation as a sociotechnical discipline spanning capabilities, human interaction, and institutional impact — with genuine independence for evaluators. A field-defining document for anyone doing or funding evals.

Sources

  • AI as Normal Technology: New paper: Emerging trends in AI agent evaluation

item.title: Willison shares an 'obituary for programming'
item.description:
Simon Willison linked to Jeremy Scheff's poignant essay capturing what coding agents have taken from career programmers who loved the puzzle of developing code: "You got paid to work on tricky little logic puzzles. The trickier the puzzle, the more you got paid... They would give us a problem and we would solve it the way we wanted. We set the strategy, we made the timeline, we defined what was and was not possible."

Willison's gloss is the kicker: if you're a programmer who thrives on building working systems and doesn't care deeply about the problems solved along the way, LLMs are the gift that keeps on giving. But if directly solving those problems was a big part of your enjoyment, the loss is very real.

The piece crystallizes a cultural shift the research world is still catching up to. The coding-agent revolution isn't just a productivity story or a jobs story — it's an identity story about what programming meant to the people who loved it, and what remains when the puzzle-solving itself is outsourced.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: My obituary for programming

item.title: Simon Willison ships LLM plugin fixes and a better echo debug tool
item.description:
A quiet maintenance day in Simon Willison's LLM tooling ecosystem. llm-tools-datasette 0.1.1 fixes a breakage caused when LLM 0.33 switched to httpx2 — the plugin used httpx without declaring it as a dependency, and now that's patched.

More interestingly, llm-echo 0.5 — the plugin that provides a fake model which just echoes prompts back — now simulates token usage counts that account for tool calls, system prompts, and reasoning tokens. It matters because Willison is stress-testing pull requests ahead of a new LLM release, and realistic usage accounting in the echo model helps catch cost-estimation bugs without spending real API calls. Small updates, but they show where the rough edges in LLM agent tooling still are: dependency hygiene and usage bookkeeping.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: llm-tools-datasette 0.1.1
  • Simon Willison's Weblog: llm-echo 0.5

item.title: Leaked draft of Anthropic's AI regulatory bill draws sharp criticism
item.description:
A purported draft of an AI regulatory bill that Anthropic is reportedly shopping to lawmakers has leaked, and Zvi Moshowitz's early read is harsh: he calls the draft unacceptable and troubling, arguing that even with its apparent bugs fixed, it would be a bad piece of legislation.

Why it matters: Anthropic has been positioning itself as the most policy-engaged of the frontier labs, and a leaked draft from them — rather than from regulators — is a sign that labs are actively trying to shape the rules they will be governed by. For researchers and practitioners, the substance of the bill matters less right now than the signal: the industry is entering a phase where companies write the first drafts of their own regulation, and early drafts deserve close scrutiny before they gain momentum.

Sources

  • The Zvi: Leaked Anthropic Draft AI Regulatory Bill Is Unacceptable and Troubling

item.title: AI code review is being rewired: "did a human read the code?" is the wrong question
item.description:
Simon Willison spotlighted a rethink of code review for the AI era, quoting Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang: "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for the real question — what could go wrong with this change, and which check, automated or human, is the right one to catch it? The sharper framing is changing when review happens: instead of a gate at the end of the road (write the code, open a PR, wait for a colleague), review now runs continuously, "more like spellcheck while you write."

Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look, catching routine mistakes early and saving team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny. It's a compact statement of how seriously the review workflow is being rewired: the bottleneck is no longer reviewer availability but deciding which checks genuinely need a human eye.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: Quoting Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang

item.title: AINews: agents are disproving polysemanticity and boosting interpretability
item.description:
Nick Cammarata is making major claims in a new Latent.Space AINews episode: AI agents are helping disprove polysemanticity — the long-standing finding that individual neurons respond to many unrelated concepts — and in doing so are greatly improving interpretability and alignment research.

If the claim holds up, it's significant: polysemanticity has been one of the core obstacles to reading neural networks' internals, and resolving it would give safety researchers a much clearer window into model behavior. That said, the feed entry gives only the episode's headline, so treat this as a pointer rather than a verdict — the episode itself is where to judge whether the evidence matches the ambition. Worth a listen for anyone tracking whether interpretability is on the verge of a step change.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: [AINews] Agents disprove Polysemanticity; greatly improve Interpretability & Alignment

item.title: Modal hits $1B ARR and a $16B Series D — NYC's newest AI infra decacorn
item.description:
Modal, the serverless AI infrastructure company, has reached $1 billion in annualized recurring revenue and closed a $16 billion Series D — tripling both usage and valuation in five months, and growing roughly 15x in a year. That makes it New York's newest AI infrastructure decacorn.

The numbers underline where the real money in AI is concentrating: not just in models, but in the sandboxed compute platforms that run them. Modal's bet is that "sandboxes are all you need" — ephemeral, isolated compute for AI workloads — and the market is now valuing that proposition at decacorn levels.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: [AINews] Modal's $1B ARR, $16B Series D makes it NYC's newest AI Infra Decacorn, 3x usage and 3x valuation in 5 months, 15x in 1 yr

item.title: Nvidia scales Indic pretraining to 2.8 trillion tokens with an open data pipeline
item.description:
Nvidia published a technical post on scaling Indic-language pretraining to 2.8 trillion tokens, along with an open data generation pipeline for building large multilingual corpora. Indic languages have historically been underserved in pretraining data, and this is one of the largest efforts to close that gap.

The open pipeline matters as much as the token count: reproducible data generation lets other teams build high-quality pretraining sets for underrepresented languages. For a research community increasingly focused on multilingual evaluation, this is genuinely useful infrastructure.

Sources

  • Hugging Face Blog: Scaling Indic Pretraining: 2.8 Trillion Tokens and an Open Data Generation Pipeline

item.title: IBM's Granite Switch 4.1: chat, decisions, and speech from one endpoint
item.description:
IBM released Granite Switch 4.1, which unifies chat, decision-making, and speech capabilities behind a single endpoint. Rather than orchestrating separate models for conversation, reasoning, and voice, teams can route all three through one interface.

It's a pragmatic enterprise play: fewer endpoints to manage, one model family to evaluate, and less plumbing in production. The "switch" framing suggests the model dynamically handles the different modes, which — if it holds up in practice — simplifies a lot of real-world agent deployments.

Sources

  • Hugging Face Blog: Granite Switch 4.1: Chat, Decisions, and Speech from One Endpoint

item.title: Chirp Pong: a two-player phone game networked through sound
item.description:
Simon Willison built Chirp Pong, a two-player competitive Pong-like game played on two separate phones, where game state is transmitted between devices as audio chirps picked up by the Web microphone API — no network, no pairing, just sound. He built it with Claude Opus 5.5 via Claude Code, adding graphical and gameplay twists beyond plain Pong.

It's a delightful proof of concept: acoustic networking as a fallback channel for local multiplayer, running in static HTML on ordinary phones. The experiment shows how fast an idea can go from "is this even feasible?" to working demo with modern coding agents — which is arguably the real story.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: Chirp Pong

item.title: Anthropic's investor day: $16.8B Q3, 11% margins, and a distillation edge
item.description:
Anthropic briefed investors ahead of its IPO, and the FT's reporting — summarized by Simon Willison — fills in the trajectory: roughly $4.8B in Q1, $11.5B in Q2, $16.8B in Q3, with adjusted operating margins of 11% excluding stock-based comp. Strikingly, Q3 brought in $1.70 of revenue for every $1 spent on compute.

That ratio is the number to watch: it suggests Anthropic's distillation and efficiency work is converting compute spend into revenue at a healthy multiple, not just burning capital for growth. As the IPO approaches, these are the economics the market will price — and they'll set the benchmark for every frontier lab's fundraising story.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO
